utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Mr. Registrar, may you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Laurie Sartorio, assisted by our intern, Emma Berry, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to my friends from the Prosecution and to everyone in the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson on behalf of General Rasim Delic, with our assistants Lejla Gluhic, Lana Deljkic, and Asja Zujo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Sir, I know you know this already by now, but it's still my duty to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, General. Your Honour, I would like to return back to the diary of the 18th -- the extract of the diary from the 18th of June of June, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You always may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, do you have your diary for June 1993 beside you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The diary is here now. It can be handed over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You showed me the notes for the 18th of June yesterday; however, I don't have it next to me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, if you could please check your diary for the entry for the 18th of June, now that you have the document.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: There seems to be no note on the 18th of June concerning any discussion about foreign volunteers in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, having just told us that, yesterday I showed you an order of General Delic to the 3rd Corps, dated the 16th of June, ordering foreign volunteers to be sent to Igman to join an independent detachment or to otherwise have their hospitality withdrawn. Is it possible that the meeting at which the Mujahedin were discussed actually took place before the 16th of June?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to verify that against the notes, starting with the day of Mr. Delic's appointment as commander. The first briefing session of the commander was on the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, if I could, perhaps, stop you there.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is it possible that the meeting at which the Mujahedin were discussed took place before the 16th of June, and you didn't record it in your diary?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is such a possibility, perhaps; however, judging by my notes and the method I used to note things down, had there been such a meeting, I believe I would have noted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to turn to a different issue. Yesterday, you were shown a document by the Prosecution, Exhibit 350 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And perhaps if we could just have the document brought up on the screen, just the front page. Your Honours, this was the document from the Zenica MUP and 3rd Corps, dated 10th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it 10th of June or 10th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise, the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, during your testimony, you stated, in relation to this document, that, "I want to reiterate that this was a joint report; however, it was drafted by the Ministry of the Interior of Zenica. It was signed by the 3rd Corps commander as well, though." And my question to you is: Do you agree that the Ministry of Interior had authority to deal with problems relating to civilians and persons who were not members of the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inter alia, that was one of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document can be put away, and I'm going to turn to another issue, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, during the first day of your testimony, you were asked by the Prosecution about changes in the ethnic composition of the ARBiH after June 1993, and you told the Court: "It began changing after some five or six months of existence of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you recall giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So that would mean that the ethnic composition of the ARBiH was already changing in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992 and early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown a Defence document, D245.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, could you just confirm for us that what we can see here is a document headed "Recommendation." It's addressed to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it's dated the 17th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could just please look at page 5 of the English version and page 2 of the Bosnian version. If we can, first of all, go down to the bottom of the pages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you confirm, General, that this recommendation, sent on the 17th of June, was sent by General Delic?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we can just go back to page 2 of the English version, and also page 1 of the Bosnian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you see a heading -- a subheading there, General, that says "Recommend"?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it correct, General, that this recommendation relates to a proposed new organisation and establishment structure of the command and control of the arms struggle and further engagement in war in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to go back to page 5 of the document in the English version and page 2 in the Bosnian. Do you see the second-from-last paragraph just above the signature of General Delic? It's the --

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: The integral part of this proposition is the schematic display of the organisation of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, in fact, if I can just read this paragraph out to you, what it states, General, is that: "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Army chart and draft decision on the organisational structure of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Ministry of Defence are integral parts of this recommendation." So does that show, General, that attached to this recommendation is an -- is something else, it's a draft decision?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a recommendation on how to structure, in terms of organisation and establishment, the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we can actually look at the draft decision, we can find it as an annex to this document. It's -- in the English version, it's on page 6; and in the B/C/S version, it's page 3. If you could just briefly look at the heading of this document, General, would you agree that this is the draft decision that we've just discussed, which is an integral part of General Delic's recommendation?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I can state that it has its legal foundation, since it was drafted by Dr. Musir Brkic, who at the time was the head of the Department of Legal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, the part that I'd like to refer you to can be found in -- on page 12 of the English version and page 5 of the B/C/S version. Now, General, the relevant part I'd like to refer you to is point 5 on this page. It's towards the bottom of the page. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you please read that out to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When appointing active servicemen and civilians employed by the army to establishment positions in administrations and departments of the Main Staff, attention shall be given to a balanced representation of the peoples of the Republic and other ethnicities who live in it. "Main Staff deputy commanders shall represent the peoples, Muslim, Serb, and Croat. The organisation and establishment of the Main Staff are determined by the Presidency of the Republic at the recommendation of the Main Staff commanders collegium."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, General, the recommendation of General Delic was issued on the 17th of June, which was only a short time after he was appointed as commander; is that so?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please see whether this document is, indeed, dated the 17th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can do that. It's on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps, if we can just show the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, the 17th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that it's clear, from the recommendation and the draft decision, that General Delic was trying to preserve the ethnic composition of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: He merely implemented the things envisaged by the Constitution, and when the organisation of the staff of the army was supposed to have been organised in the way that it would represent all of the peoples residing in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to turn to a different issue, and this concerns the video clips that you were shown relating to the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, please, could the third clip be shown again to General Delic [sic], and I'll perhaps say when it can be stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Commander of the General Staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina addressed those present."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, the first thing I'd like to ask you: We saw those video clips several times during the last few days. Could you confirm for us that at no time during the course of seeing those clips did we see any Arabic-looking men or foreigners in those clips?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I did not see any. But the way you put it, I believe it's a bit leading, if I'm using the correct term. It's very leading; however, I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, for you, General, and perhaps fortunately for me, I have the right to put these sorts of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, hold on. I may be mistaken, but I think we saw some gentlemen with white hats and black robes, did we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed, we did, Your Honour. Perhaps, we can refer back to the video clip, and we can explore this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt your cross-examination. It's just to clarify what we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just add my confusion, too, so that when you go back to the clip, you can deal with it as well, Mr. Robson. I just don't know how your question can be answered, how one confirms that people there are one race or the other, but I just -- I'm perplexed. Carry on, carry on. I also am not going to interfere with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, the men in the white robes, and this is the -- holding the guns, just to be absolutely clear, they were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade; is that so?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we show those men that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If the clip could be shown from the beginning again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Following that, the commander of the General Staff, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Rasim Delic, addressed the honourable ranks of the 7th Muslim Chivalrous Mountain Brigade and all present. "Firstly, I must convey ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just be sure I follow the question. Are we talking about the officials who are standing in front, including Mr. Delic, or are we talking about the army -- members of the army who are in white uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the initial question was based on the fact that the Trial Chamber had the opportunity to watch these clips on several occasions during the course of yesterday, I think it was. And the question directed to the General was whether, based on him seeing those clips played a number of times, whether he could identify -- whether he noticed any Arabic-looking men whatsoever. So that would be within the crowd of the soldiers or within the lineup of officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then I follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't notice anyone of that description, a foreigner. I don't see any person like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could this clip be backed up a little, please, just -- what I'd like to do is identify a frame which has a gentleman in the blue jacket with a beard, in a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's before then. It's probably as easy to run it from the beginning again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you see the gentleman there in the blue jacket with the short hair and beard, General?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us that that man is Halil Brzina?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is it right that he is a Bosniak from Bosnia-Herzegovina, or a local Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say the rest; however, I can tell you that he is a local Bosniak. I am not familiar with his biography there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Your Honours, I don't propose to have any more questions about this video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Before we leave that issue, General, we saw some of the religious men in robes and headwear. Can you confirm that they also were not Arabic gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the reis ulluma, Effendi Seric, who is the head of the Islamic religious community in Bosnia-Herzegovina. His origins may be Arabic, but it probably goes a couple of hundred years back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to turn to the transcript of the interview with General Divjak, and in particular the extract which was put on the ELMO yesterday and shown to the Trial Chamber. What I would propose at this stage is if the relevant page or pages could please be returned to the ELMO. Perhaps, please, could I have a look at the document before it goes on there. Your Honours, it's going to be necessary to look at two pages of this document. Before the document is actually put onto the ELMO, if I could perhaps begin by asking the General the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yesterday, General, the Prosecutor suggested that in this interview, it said that, and I quote: "7th Muslim Brigade is responsible to a certain extent for atrocities over non-Bosniak people." You responded that: "What I said is written here, which is that the 7th Muslim Brigade also bears responsibility." And you went on to say: "I did not know that the brigade was doing anything in contravention of the Geneva Conventions." Can you recall giving that response?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If the first page could please be put on the ELMO. If we can move down to the -- so it shows the bottom half of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, this document records what you actually said during the course of that OTP interview. Please, could you read out what you said from line 24 onwards?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: "However, there is a personal opinion of mine here, which is to state certain responsibility for the suffering of the non-Bosniak people."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can please put the next page on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It will be the top of this page.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is borne by the 7th Muslim Brigade. The 7th Muslim Brigade was a unit that have full logistical support." You know well, I suppose, that they elected Alija Izetbegovic their honorary commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So what you mentioned during this interview was "suffering"; is that so?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Suffering" and "threats."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: At no stage, then -- it's right to say, isn't it, General, that at no stage was the word "atrocities" used by you during this interview?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to be sure, are you suggesting that the interpretation is incorrect here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So instead of the word "atrocities" on line 7, it should read what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: "Suffering." And also, Your Honour, I would say it would be the Defence's position that the reference to "destruction" on line 2 is also incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And "casualties" on line 2 also?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can we have the correct interpretation of those two words also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see what is being interpreted by those words?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to explain, we've obviously read out -- the General has read out exactly what he said during that interview; and, today, it's been interpreted by professional interpreters, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just excuse me, because I was unaware of this being the issue, so I didn't pick up on what it should have been instead, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps then, please, if we could go back to the previous page, at the bottom, and we could get the General to read out again what he actually said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, please, could you repeat for the Trial Chamber what you told the investigator on that day?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: "However, there is a personal opinion of mine here, to state the responsibility for the suffering of the non-Bosniak people."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could go on and if you could just read the very next part.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is borne by the 7th Muslim Brigade." Can I add to this, to my opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- sorry, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You should ask now the witness to clarify what he was actually saying here, because it seems to me that General Divjak does say that the 7th Muslim Brigade was in some way responsible for some suffering of non-Bosniak people. So what was he talking about, and when and where did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, you've heard His Honour's question. Are you able to clarify that point, please?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, and the day before yesterday, during the interview with counsel, with counsel, I said that as far as I -- what I knew about all this, I acquired in September 1993; namely, when I went to tour the 2nd Corps, having stayed for a while in Zenica. Also, I was in touch with the people who were members of the Association of Serbian Citizens Council, and they told me about an instance of the sowing of disquiet, unrest, among the non-Bosniaks. They explained to me at that time that one of the methods of sowing fear was the way that they were carrying out their morning workouts. At that time, as regards the physical extermination, although that is too harsh a word, but as regards physical torture, I had not; namely, when I reframe from fully saying what's on my mind, that is because that is the information I gained after the war and during the processes that were conducted. In fact, one of those processes trials was conducted before this Tribunal. I seek to speak about things that I personally witnessed, not things that I heard. So in that time, 1993 and 1994, I, at that time, I had no information that the 7th Muslim Brigade, apart from the example which I gave you, tortured non-Bosniaks otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Will you pursue this issue, because if you don't, then I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't intend to ask the question -- this witness any further questions about what he's just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But, General, could you just please clarify something. What you actually -- the expression that you used during this interview was you talked about "responsibility for the suffering of non-Bosniaks." Now, the interpreter who was with you in that interview has interpreted what you said as being "the destruction of non-Bosniak people" and also as "atrocities over non-Bosniak people." Would you agree with me that that interpreter has mistranslated what you've said?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: In regard of such harsh formulations, yes. But I should like to repeat what I have just said a while ago. My information about the activities and the way the 7th Muslim Brigade was used was information which I gained after the war, and a year ago proceedings were conducted here before this very Tribunal in connection with the conduct of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I appreciate the point you're making, but the issue that we are dealing with right now is the translation of what you told the OTP in 2005. I'm going to move on to a different issue, if I may. If the witness could please be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robson, sorry for interrupting you, but I have got a problem of interpretation, myself. It seems to me that I understood the witness as saying yesterday that there is a difference between the words "Bosnian" and "Bosniak," and here in English I see that when the witness mentioned the Bosniaks. Here, in English, we have "Bosniaks"; whereas, in French, I seem to hear the word "Bosnian." But I understood that "Bosnian" was a more general term referring to all those people living in Bosnia; whereas, "Bosniak" is something more limited, and it is a word that designates a religious community, the Muslims if I understand correctly. Therefore, I would like to have some clarification on that point; and if necessary, corrections in the French transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, Your Honour, you have made a very good distinction between the Bosnians and the Bosniaks. The Professor Paul Gard, whom you probably know, actually, in seeking to explain to the French public these two concepts, explained that a "Bosnian" was a citizen of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So we have a Bosnian who is a Bosniak and a Bosnian who is a Serb and a Bosnian who is a Croat. And "Bosniaks" is a name, is a designation which the Muslims accepted as their very own from August 1993. So the 7th Muslim Brigade bears the designation of the people of the Muslims until that point in time when they took the name "Bosniak." A small mistake can be made there, because there also exists a Bosnian language. Under the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there exists three languages: The Bosnian, the Serbian, and the Croatian languages. I am not sure whether this will suffice, Your Honour, by way of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, and thank you to the interpreters in the French booth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I proceed any further, might it be possible for these two pages to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are they not already exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The documents -- I'm not asking that the whole document be put in -- tendered into evidence. I'm just talking about these specific two pages relating to the issue with which we've just discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The two pages that have just been shown are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, returning back to -- or turning to a different issue. Could the witness please be shown document D217. It's document D217. In the Bosnian version, if we can please scroll down to the bottom of the page, and perhaps just enhance the bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, can you just confirm for us that what we see here are the rules of service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the rules of service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I myself am one of the authors of these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could just look at the last page in the B/C/S and also English version. That's the right one. If you can scroll over, and it's the bottom left-hand corner in the B/C/S version we're interested in, if we can just focus on that. It's not necessary to look at the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, can you confirm for us that the date of these rules are the 1st of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What I'd like to refer your attention to is paragraph 12, which appears at page 2 on the English version and page 2 of the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Point 12 is on the right-hand side of the B/C/S version, so perhaps if we could focus on point 12 through to 16. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, in these rules, under the heading "Relations in the Army," do you see the part that says: "A superior shall be a person who, pursuant to the law, is authorised to lead or command a military unit command or institution and the persons who serve in them. The other persons in that unit, command or institution shall be subordinate." Can you see that part?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then underneath do you see where it says: "A senior shall be a person having a higher rank; and should the rank be the same or there is no rank, the senior shall be the person in a higher position"?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if I can refer you down to point 16, and that's on the next page in the English version, could you just read out point 16 to us, please?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 16: "A service-related order of a superior officer must be carried out by persons serving in the army without discussion completely, exactly, and promptly." Of course, the original says "time" or "promptly" in the Bosniak version. I'm speaking of the Serbian version. "Persons serving in the army must carry out the orders of the most senior commander present when their superior officer is absent and when it is necessary to take immediate measures to complete urgent tasks, especially in combat, emergency situations."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if you can read the last bit out, please.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean within item 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: "If a person serving in the army ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, General, I apologise. I'm not sure, perhaps, whether we were cut off. It was the part after "combat and emergency situations" from the first paragraph, the paragraph you were just reading from.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I'm reading. "If a person serving in the army does not receive an order or if an order arrives late ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, I apologise. I'll -- can I just ask you this: Does this paragraph say that: "Persons serving in the army must carry out the orders of the most senior commander present when their superior officer is absent and when it is necessary to take immediate measures to complete urgent tasks, especially in combat, emergency situations, and when re-establishing the disrupted organisation of work, order and discipline"?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, you've mentioned that you were one of the authors of these rules, so you must be very familiar with them. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very, but familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the effect of these rules was that the most senior ARBiH commander present at a location would have the authority to take immediate measures to complete urgent tasks?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all instances, he was the one who was making the decisions on that when he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the authority, then, that that commander would have would also allow him to order measures if it appeared to him that there had been either a breach of discipline or criminal offences committed by Bosnian Army soldiers; is that so?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, General, please, can you confirm that these rules of service were in force throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of service, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Please, could this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 359.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And now we come to the final topic of my questions. General, yesterday you were shown a video of a meeting that took place between representatives of the Bosnian Army and the HVO. Do you remember seeing that video?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your testimony, you mentioned that we could see Mr. Ganic, who was the president of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Mr. Zubak, who was the vice-president of the Federation; is that so?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what you told the Trial Chamber was that that video had been taken sometime after the Federation was formed; is that so?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, it's right the Federation was formed in 1994; can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that that meeting, of which we saw the video, could have taken place any time in 1994, 1995, or even in 1996, after the Dayton Agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, it was ascertained that this was done at the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to make clear that that point is disputed by the Defence, that was a fact -- that was something that was told to the Trial Chamber by the Prosecution, but it hasn't been led in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, General, sorry, just to return back to the question. It's the Defence's position that it has not been ascertained when the meeting took place. Would you agree with me that that meeting could have taken place in either -- in 1994, 1995, or even in 1996?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: But judging by the attire of those attending the meeting, it was in wintertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If it was in wintertime, does it follow, then, that it could have been winter of 1994, 1995, or even winter of 1996?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been 1995 or 1996, because the Peace Accords in Paris had already been signed by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: General Divjak, you were asked on cross-examination about your testimony with regard to the ethnic composition changing in the army, and you said: "It began towards the end of 1992 and early 1993." My question to you is this: Did the changing ethnic composition of the army continue to change over the course of the next two years or did it not change any further?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ethnic composition was changing. I'm not going to go into the reasons for that. But I can tell you in 1993 and 1992, we had three heads of administration who were of Croatian and Serbian ethnicity. But towards the end of 1994, we no longer had any heads of Staff or Chiefs of Staff or heads of administration of any other ethnicity but Bosniak. When we talk about other things, this was not a specific problem in 1992 and 1993 in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were only Bosniaks as commanders of corps in the army. Throughout the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were three commanders, commanders of battalions, who were of other ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What years are you talking about where there were three commanders of other ethnicity, just so I'm clear?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1992 and 1993; however, I want to stress, again, that I was talking about heads of administration. In 1992 and 1993, there were three of them who were of other ethnicities; and as of 1994 and onwards, all heads of administrations within the Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were of one ethnicity alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And do you include in "all heads of administrations," do you include corps commanders in that category?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Corps commanders are at a different command level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnic composition was in terms of the corps commanders in 1993, 1994, and 1995?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: All corps commanders were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And with regard to the foot soldiers, sir, do you know if -- what the ethnic composition was in 1993, 1994, 1995, in terms of the foot soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have such data, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I can tell you that, at that level, the overall figures remained the same. However, it did not reflect the amount of Serbs and Croats which remained in the territory controlled by the Government of the Republic of B and H. There's one thing that is important to mention, though. The armed forces, according to the Constitution and the Law on Armed Forces, were organised by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council, or comprised those two components. However, at the beginning of the war, the Croatian Defence Council failed to accept that part of the Law on Defence. We did, however, have four Croatian Defence Council's brigades which were part of the armed forces, together with the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What years was this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did the Croatian armed forces fight alongside the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993, 1994, and 1995?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigades I mentioned, one of them was in Sarajevo and two in Tuzla, fought alongside the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout the war. I wish to remind you that, in 1993 and 1994, the Croatian Defence Council, enjoying materiel and personnel support from the Croatian Army, actually carried out or waged a war. After the Washington Accords, there was cooperation between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council in the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked -- you were asked a question about a document signed by General Delic, and I believe your quote at page 7, line 25 says: "He merely implemented the things envisaged by the Constitution." Do you recall saying that? I probably have the wrong -- it was probably -- yes. I'm sorry. It was 7:25. Do you recall saying, referring to General Delic: "He merely implemented the things envisaged by the Constitution"?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know what document you're referring to. If you mean the law, that's one thing. As for the document signed by Delic, it's another thing. Please give me the reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It was Exhibit number 357, if the witness could be shown this exhibit again, please. Could we go to point 5 on page 12 of the English, page 12 of English, and page 5 of the B/C/S. And I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you also refer us to the transcript page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. It is page 7, line -- starting at page 7. And it's all of page 7, and the answer to the question I just quoted was at line 25. Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, sir, you were read this. Number 5 was read to you, and you were asked by my learned colleague: "And would you agree with me, General, that it's clear from the recommendation and the draft decision that General Delic was trying to preserve the ethnic composition of the ARBiH?" Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was put that way. However, what was being discussed was whether it says that the Main Staff deputy commanders should represent the peoples, Muslim, Serb, and Croat. And what I wanted to say was that what needed to be kept in mind was to reflect the ethnic composition of the peoples; that is, the army structures should reflect that. I read that from the document, and I can confirm that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like the witness to be shown, please, P01778.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And while we're waiting -- it's up on the screen. The date of this document, would you agree, is 5 August 1994? Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it says, "Sarajevo, the 5th of August, 1994."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I see this was a PT that was brought to the Defence's attention, but I'd just be grateful if Prosecuting counsel could perhaps just explain briefly what the document is before the witness answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, are you objecting to anything, or why do you want to tell the Prosecution how to conduct their proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, initially, I thought that it was a document that hadn't been mentioned to the Defence prior to the witness coming, but I see that it does appear on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, sir, if you look on the right-hand side of the first page, who this document is going to, it's going to the command post at Kakanj, commands of all the corps, all the administrations, Supreme Command, all the independent departments in the Supreme Command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says: "Sent to command post Kakanj," and the rest of the things you mentioned, "commands of all the corps ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I would also like to turn -- have the witness shown the last page, please, to see who the document is from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Army General Rasim Delic, Commander."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to the first page, please. Your Honours, I'd like to ask the witness -- there are certain parts I want.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: At the beginning, the first paragraph says: "At a meeting of representatives of the ARBiH Supreme Command and representatives of the ARBiH Islamic community, it actually set some important issues of organisation of religious life in ARBiH were discussed. It was concluded that command and control bodies in most of our army units ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: " ... successfully carry out their obligations, so as to create room for religious needs of BiH army soldiers and that the organisation of soldiers' religious life significantly contributed to higher combat morale in the units and commands, which improved combat efficiency of our army, too." Do you agree that's what's reflected in that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then the second paragraph says: "One of the essential goals of our liberation struggle is preservation of religious identity of our Bosniak people, against whom genocide is being carried out so that the roots of Islam in this area can be eradicated. The struggle for preservation of our national identity and physical survival is in its essence a struggle for preservation of Islam and BiH. At the same time, this is a struggle for full equality of all people and religions." Is that what paragraph 2 says?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Before I go on, I guess my question to you is: Did the Constitution envisage the integration of the religion of Islam and the principles that are espoused by this religion into the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Constitution does not mention any integration of the religion of Islam. It guarantees equal rights to all believers, irrespective of whether they are members of the Orthodox, Catholic, or any other church, including the religion of Islam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you reviewed this document on Sunday, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you see the word "Catholic" or "Orthodox" or "Serb" or "Croat," or anything in this document other than -- excuse me -- in this document at all, anywhere?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And now, if you go down to paragraph 4, it says: "Staff members of the Islamic community who are directly engaged in the BiH Army are completely satisfied with the stand of commanders and other key members of staff towards the organisation's needs ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry. "... towards the organisation's needs and implementation of religious life in our units and commands."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This document was written by General Delic, and he --

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. He signed it. However, it was drafted by his Morale Administration chief, the Administration for Morale and Religious Issues, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to move that this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 360.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson, can I suggest that you hold what you want to say until after the break. We're five minutes into the break time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'd be grateful for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no issue to raise. Thank you. We've sorted it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I ask the document be admitted in evidence. That was my last request, and it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was admitted as Exhibit 360.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just one more question at page 21 of the transcript, lines 23 through 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown this particular -- it's in English. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The question to you from my learned colleague was -- it was in reference to the section on command and control in the document that you were shown, and he said: "Now, the authority, then, that that commander would have would also allow him to order measures if it appeared to him that there had been either a breach of discipline or criminal offences committed by Bosnian Army soldiers; is that so?" And you answered: "Yes, yes." My question to you, sir, is: What effect does this provision have on the responsibilities and duties of a superior commander?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: By issuing an order, a superior officer issues tasks to his subordinate. The subordinate, in turn, is duty-bound to submit a report on the measures taken pursuant to that order. If he was unable to implement such tasks, he was supposed to seek help in resolving the matter with the commander. In all situations, subordinate officers, first of all, have to report on the reception of tasks. They also have to state that they understood them; and if not, they should ask clarification. And then once the task is completed, and it is always within a deadline, they have to report back to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. My question to you is not about the responsibilities of the subordinate officer, but of the subordinate's superior commander. What effect does this provision have on the responsibilities of the commander above the commander -- commanding officer that is provided for in that provision?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Judge, I wanted to start replying this way as an introduction to the system of command and control. The commander is duty-bound to take measures against a person who failed to implement tasks as they were set out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If the intermediary commander fails to take measures, what effect does that have or what responsibilities does that impose on the superior commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, reference has been made to an "intermediary commander." There's been no reference to such a person earlier in the testimony. I wonder if this question could be rephrased, perhaps, to avoid any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Robson, is it not so that the army is a hierarchy and this deals with the rule that you referred to? It deals with commander and subordinate. Now, the question is: Given the hierarchy in the army, what happens if this man fails to do -- this commander fails to do his job? What are the responsibilities of the higher commander? Isn't that legitimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate the reason why my learned friend is asking these questions. Perhaps, if we can let the witness answer, and if he understands, fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, whether he understands is another matter. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would like to -- may I rephrase the question, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may. You are not bound to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Just one second. May I have a moment, Your Honour, to speak to my senior colleague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: General Divjak, the Judge just asked -- well, proposed a question: Given the hierarchy in the army, what happens if a subordinate - well, this isn't his words - but what happens if a subordinate fails to act, fails to do his duties? What are the responsibilities of the higher commander? That is the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought your question was: What are the responsibilities of the higher commander if the intermediary commander fails to perform his duties by disciplining the subordinate?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's the question, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, phrase it correctly so that the witness understands exactly what you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: General, what are the responsibilities of the higher commander if the intermediary commander fails to perform the duties -- his duties of disciplining a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any commander that had ordered something, irrespective of the level of command and control, if his subordinate failed to implement the task, he is bound to take measures as envisaged in the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Divjak. We understand that, and we know that perfectly well, and hence the question is put. The question now is: That commander has failed to discipline a subordinate. What are the responsibilities of the superior commander? That first level that you are answering to, we understand, and that has been answered. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a level in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let me tell you what the question to you is, sir. You have a subordinate who is given instructions by a superior. The subordinate fails to carry out the instructions, okay, and the superior fails to discipline the subordinate. What are the responsibilities of the higher superior to this intermediary commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the question. Are you able to answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The higher superior commander needs to take measures, disciplinary measures, as stated in the law, as I said already. The first thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said that already, so you can't answer the question. Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We have no further questions, Your Honour, of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Yes, Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions myself. Let me start with the last topic raised, the issue of the responsibility of the commander. During the classes you followed as part of your training as a military man, did you study international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, commanders have followed that type of course, and they are made aware of the principles of humanitarian law, including the responsibility of the commander, who is supposed to report matters to the operation zones. I'm talking about the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we were taught.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another topic. Yesterday, during examination-in-chief, at some point, if I'm not mistaken - the parties may correct me if I'm wrong - but it seems to me that you spoke about the El Mujahid Detachment. Speaking about that detachment, you stated that they took part in the fighting in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. Am I mistaken or is it what you stated yesterday?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not mistaken. However, I said that it was part of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I wanted to find out. I wanted to understand whether the fact that they took part in the fighting in the area of responsibility, as you said: "According to me, 'of the 3rd Corps' meant that they were part of the 3rd Corps. They were incorporated in the 3rd Corps." Thank you very much for your answer. Thus, I have a few more questions to put to you regarding something raised during cross-examination conducted by Mr. Robson. You said that it was very difficult to communicate in Bosnia during the war, throughout the war, during the siege of Sarajevo and other events. I got the impression that you wanted to stress something. I might be mistaken. But on two occasions, you stated that these problems in communications were specifically related to Srebrenica and Gorazde. I would like you to explain a bit more about these problems in relation to what you, yourself, stated earlier during the examination-in-chief, when you explained that there were regular meetings once or twice a month with the commanders in the field. You stated that reports were prepared. And regarding the difficulties in communications in the area that is of interest to us here, I would like to know how this made it difficult for commanders in the field and commanders in the operation zones to communicate.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about 1992. No one from the Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina could go out into the field, the territory of, for instance, the 3rd or the 2nd or the 4th Corps, because Sarajevo was blockaded. And it was only with approval, permission, from the forces of UNPROFOR, from the commander of the UNPROFOR, that some people could get out of Sarajevo in order to maintain links on the ground. But some people were running across the airport under fire or in the thick of combat. Actually, it did convey certain directives to the areas of Zenica, Tuzla, and Bihac. In 1993, the situation improved, at which time members of the Staff could get out using the tunnel and, therefore, meet more often with their subordinated units. You could see from General Delic's decision that, in order to improve the functional role of the Staff, there were formed command posts, or rather, a command post outside. Up to that time, there had been many obstacles, many impediments to the obtaining of genuine, correct information. The Staff of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army could liaise only with a part of the command, so only of the corps commands, not of most of the units. They could actually maintain communications with these by way of a satellite telephone, and the satellite telephone, regardless of the protection system, was monitored by the aggressor. When I said that we had problems, I meant also during the execution of combat activities because the aggressor, the enemy, would often hit the command post office and unit and impair the system of communications, the repair of which took several days, so that the command-and-control system improved from the end of 1993 onwards. I should also like to draw your attention, once again, to the fact that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, appreciating the problems associated with the execution of defence operations in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, ordered the Chief of Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Halilovic, to, together with a group of officers of the Main Staff, set up a forward command post at Mount Igman, but that was never actually done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer, for this very detailed and very clear answer of yours. I'm sorry, but I have an additional question. To your knowledge, and we are talking about the 7th Muslim Brigade we saw in a video clip both yesterday and today, in that respect, were there, to your knowledge, foreigners among the foot soldiers of this detachment? I'm not talking about the officers. I'm talking about the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this bit of information about foreigners as being comprised within the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yesterday, you stated that the 7th Muslim Brigade was not characterised by its religious composition. I have a question thus: Why was there a ceremony organised, a ceremony where religious Muslim leaders took part and delivered a religious speech?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, Your Honour, I'm not quite sure that this is what I said, that I said that it did not have a religious component, that is. I should like to explain that unit, which essentially was formed in this way, honoured religious rules in the unit and abided by them, but that was the right of those people, the right -- their right to respect regulations which regulate Islam in that unit and during the execution of combat missions; namely, that unit did feature elements of respect for the religion of Islam more than was the case in other units in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, General. As you're aware, the trial here is against General Delic, among other things, for not taking the necessary measures to prevent or punish crimes that were committed by -- that were alleged to be committed by some of the members of the Mujahedin. So this is why the legal matters are relevant; and as they had not been fully covered, I have some extra questions relating to the legal aspects. And the first question I want to put to you is: What exactly was the field of responsibilities between you and General Siber? I understand that the two of you were the immediate subordinates of General Delic. What did you deal with and what did Siber deal with; do you remember? And if you don't understand my question, let me be more direct. Which of you were supposed to look after the legal matters; that is to say, to ensure that there was a proper system for disciplining or prosecuting breaches of the law? Was that you or was that Siber?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither one of us. As far as I know, in the job description of our actual positions, it was said that we were to represent the commander in certain tasks that he delegated to us. I saw from these documents that were shown that, on several occasions, I even attended Presidency sessions, where I represented the commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As for our duties in the Staff itself, they were divided between us. We shared responsibility in terms of coordinating responsibilities, activities; for instance, I was in charge of the Operations Centre, the Combat Arms Administration, the Moral Guidance Administration, the Personnel Administration. On the other side, Mr. Siber, being a technical officer, he was not responsible for, but responsible for coordinating logistics, organisational, mobilisation, and personnel affairs. With the commander, who initially was Mr. Sefer Halilovic and later Mr. Delic, we were to consider together issues which were related to the organising and execution of the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was our obligation to give him suggestions and proposals to assist him in making certain specific decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The question would then be: If you and Siber together did ensure that there was a system in place that would enable the imposition of disciplinary measures or prosecution against any member of the ABiH who acted in violation of the laws that were applicable to the members of the ABiH, including, of course, the international humanitarian law, the Geneva Conventions, the additional protocols, did you, together with Siber, ensure that there was such a system in place and that it was functioning?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not following those issues - at least, I was not. I don't know about Siber - those issues which relate to respect for regulations and laws, because they were within the ambit of the legal administration, legal affairs administration. And the bulk of the documents that were written were written by a person, by a man who was in sovereign command of the law, and he had defended his doctorate thesis before the war and was a well-known expert on the subject in the army. We had instructions or a directive that actually envisaged the procedure to be followed in instances of disciplinary breaches, setting out very specifically what a breach of discipline was, what a failure to issue -- to execute a task was, what a refusal to carry out the task was. And the paragraphs also specified the relevant ambits, the relevant authorities in such instances. This actually made it possible to establish a system which would ensure that the decisions and orders of superiors would be complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Just out of curiosity, what was the name of the gentleman who was in charge of the legal affairs; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's definitely Dr. Musir Brkic. In fact, I said a while ago that the document which was cited here as having been signed by Mr. Delic, on the 16th of June, 1993, had been drawn up, written by Dr. Musir Brkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So your testimony is that you didn't deal with this because that was the responsibility of Dr. Brkic, but did you know if a system was in place? I understand that you didn't deal with it, but do you remember if there was a system, and were there military courts and did they function?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were set up immediately in 1992, in July or August, I believe, and they also fell under the competence of the administration which was a superior agency. There was, namely, the Administration for Legal Affairs which had, within the Ministry of Defence, a legal affairs administration superior to it, and they cooperated in order to produce joint documents. In other words, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina insisted, through the legal administration of the Ministry of Defence, that specific legal regulations be voted in, in the Presidency and by the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure you are aware that there is often a difference between what the written word is and what the actual facts are, and so my question was really if you could remember any trials ever being held against members of the ABiH who had committed violations of the laws. I don't ask you to give us any specific example, but my question was merely a general one, if your recollection is that there was actually a system and that it worked well and that trials were held every now and then.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the first prosecutions were against those in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who violated the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's then try to narrow in a bit on the issues that are relevant to this case, because you said, in response to a question put by Judge Lattanzi, that the El Mujahedin Detachment was a part of the 3rd Corps. My question is, then: What does this imply, in terms of control over the combat actions that were carried out by the El Mujahedin Detachment? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand whether he was directly linked to the 3rd Corps Command -- whether it was directly connected to the 3rd Corps Command or connected to one of the brigades. Now, irrespective of what variant was in question, whatever that or any other unit did, if that was in contravention of the Geneva Conventions and other rules of war, the measures were to be undertaken by the first superior, the first next superior. That means that if it was a part of a specific brigade, the commander of that brigade was responsible for such steps. If it was comprised within the corps directly as a unit, then the person responsible for taking measures was the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, General, the problem we have here in this trial - and this is why you are testifying to us - is that the allegation has been made that the El Mujahedin Detachment was acting so independently that, at least in fact, on the tactical level, it was not a part of the 3rd Corps. It acted very independently. It acted perhaps along with combatants of the 3rd Corps, but it was not under the control of the 3rd Corps. This is the issue which we are trying to find out whether this is right or wrong. So my question to you is, first of all: Were you aware of the possibility of any question being raised about the control over the El Mujahedin Detachment, or is this completely news to you?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything in this regard, namely, in what way the El Mujahid Detachment was engaged, is something that I found out for the first time and did not know before; namely, the reports which I saw here, the documents that were shown to me here obviously demonstrate that it did not function according to the orders issued it by the superior command. The joint report by the police of Zenica and the 3rd Corps commander also shows, and still shows, that the unit is not functioning as part of the 3rd Corps. I was not shown documents here from which it could be seen whether anyone and in what way took the prescribed measures vis a vis the commander of that unit, because the commander of that unit is responsible for the conduct of his combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us leave aside for the moment the question of whether any action was taken, because my first interest is to know whether you, at any point in 1993, received information that there were disciplinary problems between -- or disciplinary problems in relation to the control over the El Mujahedin Detachment. Was that ever brought to your attention at any point in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- in our Operations Centre, we did not receive such information from the 3rd Corps in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You're saying that you did not?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: We who were there in the Staff, at the Staff in Sarajevo, namely, the group that had morning, every morning, discussions and analyses of events unfolding on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did not receive such information, including me, myself. At that time, we received no such reports from the subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, I think, but I may be wrong, but I think there was. We had been given information during this trial that a complaint or a request or a letter was sent by the UNHCR, I think, by Mr. Akashi, to the Supreme Command of the ABiH, regarding an alleged violation committed against Croats by foreign parts of the ABiH or people fighting in Bosnia. And I think we also have seen - but I can ask the parties to confirm this - that we've also seen that actually General Delic responded to that letter by Mr. Akashi. So this suggests that there must have been some discussions about irregularities committed by foreigners; but as far as you can recall, this was not the case. Is that how I should understand you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know this is a sensitive issue, Defence counsel intervening during Judges' questions, but if perhaps I could just be given the opportunity to correct the record on two facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Absolutely, sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The letter that was sent from the UN institution was from Mazowiecki, and the response actually came back from the president. It wasn't General Delic that responded back. And just for the final purposes of clarification, General Delic wrote to the president, so his response to President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying this. I'm grateful to you. Simply, my recollection was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I don't know if the Prosecution have any comments to make on our clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Let me just look. I think it says, yes, General Delic wrote to the president and the president then wrote to Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sartorio. This clarifies the matter insofar as apparently there was some communication at the higher level, but please let me hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter has to do with the events in the Neretva Valley. I've read it, and Mr. Mazowiecki sought explanation. Mr. Izetbegovic wrote the report, and it was forwarded to Mr. Silajdzic, who was the prime minister. This is what I managed to gather from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, then, General, I'm not sure how I should now understand your testimony, because, on the one hand, you are telling me that you never received any information about any irregularities committed by foreigners who were fighting either as part of or along with the ABiH; and yet, on the other hand, you tell me that you do recall that there was this letter from Mazowiecki and that it was responded by the president through General Delic. So was it just a different case, or how am I to understand what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it involved the Grabovica case in October 1993 when Mr. Mazowiecki wanted to receive reports, and he had information on certain contact -- conduct which was not in keeping with the Geneva Conventions. It was independently of the issue discussed here as to what was going on with the El Mujahid unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies, of course, the question.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My final question, then, would be if you recall ever having discussed the issue of crimes committed or allegedly committed by members of the El Mujahedin with General Delic. Was that ever a subject of discussion between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with me. Mr. Delic and I did not discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just start with the topic that you have been discussing with Judge Harhoff, just for my own clarification. And the first question I want to ask is: Was Mr. Musir Brkic a member of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the head of the Legal Affairs Administration within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I can tell you that he was also an adviser for legal matters, even when Mr. Halilovic was commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
