utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have satisfied me. You mentioned also that there were prosecutions against those who violated Geneva Conventions. Are you able to give us examples, one or two?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1993 or in early 1994, there was a proceedings against part of the members of the 10th Mountain Brigade in Sarajevo who were suspected of having killed several citizens of Serbian origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know the results of those proceedings?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, two were sentenced to -- to nine and ten years imprisonment, respectively. One was tried in absentia. Last year, he was taken into custody finally, and the proceedings are still ongoing in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At page 45 today, lines 7 to 10, you said: "I was not shown documents here," and I underlined the word "here," "... from which it could be seen that anyone in any way took the prescribed measures, vis a vis the commander of that unit, because the commander of that unit is responsible for the conduct of his combatants." You remember saying that to the question?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I said I emphasised the word "here." My question to you is: Are you aware of any documents, outside of here, that deal with that situation?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, out of the documents shown to me here, two-thirds of them I had never seen before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So can I interrupt you? Just that prefix doesn't go to answering my question. I'm not asking you about documents that you saw here. I'm wanting to know about documents that you are aware of outside of this place and do you have any knowledge of whether prescribed measures were ever taken in the circumstances that you are being asked here?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So you have no knowledge of any prescribed measures by way of prosecution being taken against the El Mujahid Detachment members. Thank you. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 359. At page 21 of the transcript today, lines 22 to 25, you were asked by Mr. Robson: "Now, the authority, then, that that commander would have also allow him to order measures if it appeared to him that there had been either a breach of discipline or criminal offences committed by Bosnian Army soldiers; is that so?" Now, at that time, you were discussing this exhibit that is being shown on the screen. On a reading of the paragraph that Mr. Robson was asking you a question about, I did not see the words "criminal activities" or "criminal offences" or "crime." I saw the word "discipline." And what I do want to find out from you is: Does this specific paragraph that was being referred to here, does it deal also with criminal offences or does it deal with disciplinary matters only? I'm sorry. I'm not able to remember the paragraph that was being discussed at the time. I think it is paragraph 16, yes, where it says: "A service-related order of a superior officer must be carried out by a persons serving in the army without discussion, completely, exactly, and promptly. Persons serving in the army must carry out the orders of the most senior commander present when their superior officer is absent and when it is necessary to take immediate measures to complete urgent tasks, especially in combat, in emergency situations, and when re-establishing the disrupted organisation of work, order, and discipline." That's where the word "discipline" comes. Now, I didn't -- or let me ask you: Do you understand this paragraph to also deal with criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the armed forces, there used to and still exists the rule or rules on military discipline, which regulated the issues encompassed by your question as well. Perhaps, we could use these rules in trying to establish which are the issues pertaining to military discipline and which are the competencies of different command levels and type of responsibility. It is clearly prescribed what level and what commander and what type of measure or punishment he can issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Unfortunately, I don't normally understand complicated answers. That's why I try to phrase my questions in such a way that I get a very simple, straightforward answer. And I'm going to ask the question once more, and could you please give me a very simple and straightforward answer. The answer that I expect you to give me is either a "yes" or a "no." Now, my question is, and I want to repeat the question as I put it, so I must stop this to get back to my question. My question was: "Do you understand this paragraph to also deal with criminal offences?" That was my question, very simple, one fact, and you're going to answer "yes" or "no," and I'll understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then I understand what that detailed answer meant. I have no further questions for you. Questions by Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Please bear with me a second. Further cross-examination by Mr. Robson:

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: General Divjak, just starting with His Honour Judge Moloto's last question, we've discussed paragraph 16 of these rules, which says that: "Persons serving in the army must carry out the orders of the most senior commander present when their superior officer is absent and when it is necessary to take immediate measures to complete urgent tasks, especially in combat, emergency situations, and when re-establishing the disrupted organisation of work, order, and discipline." If a senior commander at a location discovered that a subordinate member of the Bosnian Army had committed a criminal act, would the language of this text, which refers to discipline, enable that senior commander to take action against the subordinate?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how I understand your question, and in that case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'd like to refer back to some questions that were referred to you by His Honour Judge Harhoff. You were asked about the delegation of tasks or duties by the commander to the deputy commanders. Is it right to say that when tasks or duties were delegated by the commander to his deputy commanders, those tasks or duties then become the responsibility of the deputy commanders? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but within the scope of the commander's order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be particularly so if the commander delegated a task or duty to a deputy commander in the field?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you just bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: General Divjak, Her Honour Judge Lattanzi asked you about the ceremony that we saw involving the 7th Muslim Brigade, and she asked you a question about the religious speech. Is it right that during the Second World War, the Eastern Bosnian Muslim Brigade protected Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point that we're making is that the prefix attached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, wait a minute. You are now going to explain your question. You are not responding to the objection, and the objection is precisely so that your question must not be put, and therefore it must not be explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the purpose of the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I concede that. I withdraw that question, and if I could rephrase it in hopefully a better manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The video that we saw and the discussions we've had during your testimony have related to the 7th Muslim Brigade. I mentioned a moment ago that Eastern Bosnian Muslim Brigade, which is accepted was not functioning during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but would you accept, General, that the prefix "Muslim" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then, Mr. Robson, if that Eastern Bosnian Brigade did not function during this war and has never been raised in evidence, what is the relevance of your question? That's the objection of the Prosecution, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just on that final point, General, would you agree with me that the prefix "Muslim" is really not so important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we're talking about the 7th Muslim Brigade here, Your Honour, not the Eastern Bosnian Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I object. Perhaps he can -- Defence counsel can again re-ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Put your question in full, sir, a non-objectionable question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson, ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move on, and this is my last point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: General Divjak, during the proofing session several days ago with the Prosecution, and during the course of your testimony over the last few days, you were shown a number of documents which mentioned the El Mujahid Detachment. Now, not so long ago, in response to one of the questions of the Judges, you said: "Everything in this regard is something that I found out for the first time." I wish to refer you to what you told the Prosecution during that proofing session, a note of which was supplied to Defence, and it was recorded there from that session that it was your opinion that the Mujahedin were never incorporated into the ARBiH, to your knowledge, not even by the war's end. It's right, isn't it, what you told the Prosecution during that proofing session?

utterances.speaker: Jovan Divjak [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. Mr. Divjak, this brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. Let me take this opportunity, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, to thank you for taking time off your very busy schedule. I believe you must be a busy person, even though you may be retired, to come and testify. And having done so, I just want to say you are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine this is a convenient time to take the break. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours. But just before we break, the Prosecution, immediately after the break, calls Enver Berbic, and so perhaps he can be brought into the courtroom at the commencement of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we move into private session for just a short while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take the break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Our colleague, Mr. Menon, will be leading this witness in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, would you state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: My name is Enver Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 18th of November, 1957, in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berbic, were you ever a member of the Administration of the Military Security Service of the Main Staff of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when did you join the Military Security Service Administration?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I joined the Military Security Service Administration, or rather, was appointed to it in July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter didn't hear the year. Could the witness please approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, the interpreter did not hear the year that you stated that you joined the Military Security Service Administration, and the interpreter also requested that you speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. And when you joined the Military Security Service Administration, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I was based, or rather, that part of the administration was based, at the Kakanj command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. And when you joined -- when you joined the Military Security Service Administration, who was the chief of that administration?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: When I joined the Military Security Service Administration, the chief of the administration was General Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where was Mr. Jasarevic based?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the administration and of Mr. Jasarevic was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. Can you describe how the administration of the Military Security Service was organised?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I will try to describe it because I do not remember the exact details of the establishment structure, but I do remember that the Military Security Administration had departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you name those departments?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The first department was for counterintelligence affairs or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you know what the other --

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The second department was for staff security and military police affairs, and the third department was the analytical affairs department. These departments, in turn, had divisions or sections. I do not remember what sections the first department comprised; but the department to which I belonged, there was a section for staff security affairs and a section for military police affairs, as well as a general affairs section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you clarify which department you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I was appointed to the section of staff security and military police affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where were the heads of these departments based?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The heads of these departments were based in Sarajevo; but as the need arose, they would also relocate to the Kakanj command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you also clarify which section of the staff security and military police department you worked in?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I worked in the section for staff security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just want to go back and -- go back to an answer that you'd given earlier. You indicated that Mr. Jasarevic was the chief of the Military Security Administration. Can you -- what was Mr. Jasarevic's first name?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: His first name was Jusuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Berbic. Now, you indicated that you worked in the section for staff security affairs. Who was your immediate superior in that position?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the chief of the section for staff and security affairs, Mr. Refik Cesko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where was Mr. Refik Cesko based?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: At the time when I arrived at the Kakanj command post, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, in Kakanj, was there a particular building in which you were based; and if so, do you know the name of that building?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: We were based together with the other administrations and other departments in a building which was actually a motel, and the motel's name was "Sretno."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And while you were based in Kakanj, were you always located in this particular building that you've referred to as Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime in mid-1995, we moved to a building which was actually a private house not far from the Sretno Motel, and we had our rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. Now, how many people worked within the Military Security Service Administration in Kakanj during your time there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The number varied. It changed from situation to situation, but mainly, as a rule, there would be three to four men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And which departments of the Military Security Service Administration did these three to four people work in?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: From the first department, there was one representative. From my own department, there were two of us, and there were one or two from the military police section, which is to say also from my department. Occasionally, this number would change; namely, that number would occasionally increase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you -- what you're referring to when you say "the first department"?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: From the first department, there would be someone who dealt with counterintelligence protection of the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What was the name -- when you say "first department," what was the name of that department? What was the formal name of that department?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I have already said that I don't know the exact name, but, more or less, it was department for counterintelligence protection or for counterintelligence affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. Can you explain to us now what the function -- what function the Military Security Service Administration, that part of it that was based in Kakanj, what function it served?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Well, in its work, a part of the department at the Kakanj command post focused on staff security and military security work, meaning security checks of members that would be recruited for the needs of the units or for the needs of the General Staff; also maintaining records on passes and on entries and exits to and from the Kakanj command post; monitoring -- or rather, escorting convoys. We were the ones who did the organising, and the actual escorting was done by the military police; security -- provision of security for the command post and all the facilities within it. We participated in the actual -- in the preparation of the actual plans, and the actual support and security provision was provided by the military police unit. We also participated to the compiling of a part of the report -- of the reports that would be addressed to the addressees that we had in Sarajevo. I believe, one of those addressees was the Presidency in Sarajevo. We participated in the work of the Operations Centre at the Kakanj command post, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "reports," what kind of reports are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: These were regular, daily combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. Did General Delic maintain an office at Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: In Kakanj, at -- in a facility that we called "DC," there were some rooms which were intended for Commander Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "DC," what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: This abbreviation actually stands for "Distribution Centre." That is a company that used to be there prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And beyond General Delic, who else was based -- was there anyone else that had an office at the distribution centre?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Apart from General Delic, the Chief of Staff, General Hadzihasanovic, also had his offices on the first floor of the distribution centre, and for a while also some people from the Operations Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where, in relation to General Hadzihasanovic's office, was General Delic's office?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Well, that will take some remembering, if you'll bear with me. I believe that they were quite close to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P01832. If we could get the whole document on the screen, at least the whole -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I have to note the remark that this is the first time that I see this document, apart from when I was shown it by the investigators, so that I can just read what it is about. This is a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And for the record, what's the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The 8th of November [as interpreted], 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Are you sure that it's November? Can you look at it again?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: No, no. This is October.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The interpreter made the mistake. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. And which corps is this document originating from?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: It says here "3rd Corps Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note, for the record, that the translation doesn't indicate the corps. But if Your Honour were to -- Your Honours were to refer to the B/C/S version of the document, at the upper left-hand part of the document, second line, I believe that's what the witness referred to when I put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berbic, I want to refer you now to the upper part of the document on the right-hand side of it. That part of the document indicates that this document was intended for -- one of the recipients of this document was to be the command post in Kakanj. Based upon your experience in Kakanj, what would be -- what would happen to a document such as this once it reached that command post?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Well, specifically in regard of this particular date, I have no experience, because this was something that was sent immediately after I had come and I was not versed in these things. But generally speaking, reports like these would come to the Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what would happen once the document arrived at the Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Other documents and similar documents would also come there; then the representatives of the different administrations at the Kakanj command post, as well as those who were in charge of these things, would read these reports; then everybody would process a number of reports in line with their particular segment, which was their -- which they were in charge of; and then they would compile a consolidated report which would be submitted to the superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "other documents and similar documents," can you clarify what relationship those other documents and similar documents would have to a daily combat report such as this?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: This is a regular daily combat report of one corps. I don't remember how many there were then, at that time, how many directly subordinated units to the Staff of the Supreme Command there were, that is, but they all had to submit such reports, these reports, in this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And then the consolidated report, what would be done with the consolidated report once it was prepared?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I say that it would be submitted to the superiors. It would be submitted to the Presidency; and if I remember correctly, I can't claim that with certainty, it was also submitted to the commander in Sarajevo and perhaps to some other addresses as well which I cannot recall at this moment. This was a sublimated report of all the reports which were received from different quarters at the Kakanj command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "the command in Sarajevo," can you indicate -- can you just clarify whom you're referring to, the person that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I am referring to Commander Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if General Delic were to be in Kakanj, do you know how -- the process by which the document -- the consolidated report would be transmitted to him?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I do not remember that, so that I could only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could move the document, the B/C/S version of the document, a little bit to the right, and if we could scroll down on the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, I'm going to refer you to the section, it's labelled "Number 2" and it says "Our Forces," if you could read the third sentence under that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I'll note for the record that the sentence THAT Mr. Berbic is going to read on the English version of the document, that carries on to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And the sentence begins: "The units and the command," if you could just read that.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: "The units and the command of OG3-North are performing the link-up of defence lines between the ..." I can't see the number, but it says "...Light Brigade and the El Mujahid Detachment. And the command of the 319th Mountain Brigade is preparing for attack," combat activity, "on the Cungar facility," if I pronounced that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask this document be tendered into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown Exhibit P02008.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you indicate again what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: It says here in the document's title "Regular Daily Combat Report."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, for the record, can you just indicate what the date of the document is?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The date is the 3rd of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And from which -- from which corps is this document coming -- originating?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of what is written here, this document was sent from the Command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I'll note that this document is addressed to the command post in Kakanj. You've just indicated a process that regular daily combat reports would go through once they arrived there. Would that same process apply to this particular combat report?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: There are changes here in respect to the previous document. That one bore the designation "Supreme Command Staff," and here it says "the General Staff of the ARBiH," and the document is addressed to the Operations Centre. This "OC" which is indicated in the documents stands for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But this document is addressed to Kakanj. Do you agree with me or do you disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was addressed to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you indicate if -- to the extent that the process that would apply to this document, to the extent that it would differ from the process that would apply to the other document upon arrival in Kakanj, can you explain what that difference may be, if any?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I cannot explain this difference with certainty because I do not recall the period, and then I did not participate in the processing of reports that concerned the Military Security Service, as far as the first, the previous document is concerned, that is. And as regards this document, all the reports would flow into the Operations Centre. I am talking about regular daily combat reports. They would be sent by the directly-subordinated units, and then they would arrive at the Operations Centre. There, a team consisting of representatives of administrations that were in charge of the individual chapters in this report would examine all the reports; and then what was of the essence and the most important, the gist of these things would then go into the joint report and be the substance of the joint report. This completed report would then be submitted to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And just for the sake of clarification, can you indicate, to the best of your knowledge, whom those -- whom the addressees in Sarajevo would be?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I believe that such reports would be sent to Sarajevo, to Commander Delic, and the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask that we move to page 2 of the B/C/S version of this document and page 3 of the English version of the document. And, Your Honour, I would refer the witness to the last sentence of the first paragraph, and the equivalent of that in the English version is the last sentence of the second paragraph under the section entitled "Situation and Activities of the 3rd Corps Forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, can you read out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. First of all, I believe the questions that were already posed were legitimate. However, I would object to this one, since the Prosecutor did not establish the foundation of the witness's knowledge. We don't know whether the witness knows anything about the deployment of this specific unit and its activities. First of all, we have to establish whether he is familiar with that and then follow up with the questions. As for the document itself, we, as well as you, can read for yourselves what is stated therein, and the witness is not needed here to read it for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand the objection, Madam Vidovic. If the witness can deal with this document, he can be asked anything in the document and he can tell us if he does know or does not know. Why do you want to preempt him telling us whether he does know or doesn't know anything that is in the document, if you don't object to him going through the document and you object to a specific matter in the document? I don't understand that objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am objecting against questions being put to the witness without a foundation being laid, and the Prosecutor did the same with the previous document. He merely asked the witness to read out what is stated therein, without establishing any foundation; although, the witness himself said, concerning that last document, that he knows nothing about that and that he saw it for the first time during proofing. And now, again, we are in the situation of the same kind. There was no foundation as to whether the witness knew anything at all about the combat activities or the El Mujahid Detachment. He's only being asked to read it for the transcript. My objection, thus, is, first of all, to establish any foundation, then the link to this witness, and then to put a question. And we can all read the document for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Madam Vidovic. I now understand you. Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the guidelines that were issued by the Chamber set the standard in order to tender the document into evidence of showing a relation between the document and the witness. I think I've done that. I was simply having the witness -- I wanted to simply have the witness recite a passage from the document which is relevant and which speaks for itself. If the Defence wants to contest that by putting questions to the witness about his knowledge in relation to that specific passage, I think that they can do that in cross-examination. I'm not asking the witness to give his opinion on it. So as long as the document is in evidence or the foundation has been laid for the document to be tendered into evidence, I think it's legitimate for the witness to simply recite a particular passage to assist Your Honours in seeing the relevance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to read the foundation you laid for this document. You said, sir: "Do you see the document in front of you?" "Yes, I do." "Can you indicate again what type of document it is? "It says here in the document, the document's title, 'Regular Daily Combat Report.'" "And for the record, can you indicate what is the date of the document?" "The date is the 3rd." "And from which corps is the document coming -- originating?" "Well, on the basis of what is written here, this document was sent from the..." That's the answer. "And I note that this document is addressed to the command post in Kakanj." That's you asking. "You're just indicated a process that regular daily combat reports would go through once they arrived there. Would that same process apply to this particular combat report?" Is that the foundation you're saying you laid for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour. If this witness can speak to the route that this document would take once it arrived in Kakanj and what would be done with this document once it arrived there, and how further reports would be compiled based upon this document, I think that's a sufficient relation between the document and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I respond? There needs to be a specific link between this document and the witness. The witness spoke in principle about the procedure that documents went through. As for this specific document, I haven't heard the witness say that he knows of it or that he had received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that's the nub of Madam Vidovic's objection, Mr. Menon. Do you have anything to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a regular daily combat report. So these documents would have been coming in to Kakanj on a daily basis, and so I'm not sure if this witness is in a position to frankly remember every document that he might have seen, especially a document that was coming into Kakanj on a daily basis, if he would be able to remember specifically the content of each of those documents. And so in that regard, I would think that it's legitimate to at least have the witness describe the process that these types of daily documents would take once they arrived in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I? This is precisely our problem as well. We are not quite certain whether the witness can recall each and every document. That is why it is important to lay a foundation in order to be able to examine this witness as to each and every document or any document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, what was your question when Madam Vidovic first objected?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't actually hear the question that you posed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I haven't switched on my microphone. My question was: What was your question when Madam Vidovic first objected?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I was actually directing the witness to the -- to a relevant portion of the text of this document, and I was going to have the witness read that text for the record. And I'll just note, again, that I was of the view that I had laid a proper foundation for the document to be tendered into evidence, and that's why I waited until this -- until that point to actually have him -- and that's why I waited until that point to have him recite the -- recite the particular passage. But I didn't actually indicate which specific part of the document he was to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, are you interested in the procedure of the filing of this document only or are we going to be addressing the contents as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, not through this witness, and I think this witness can certainly speak to the procedure that was applied to these documents, and I think that's -- that's a sufficient basis for them to be tendered into evidence. But there will certainly be other witnesses who will be able to speak -- who may not be able to speak to this specific document but will at least be able to speak to events that have a relationship to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But my question was: If there is any part of the contents of this document that we need to discuss with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your point is that this is a document that, in the course -- the normal course, would have arrived at the Kakanj forward command in the department that this gentleman worked in; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I haven't put that question -- I haven't put that particular question to the witness, but the witness was aware of the -- of the procedure that was applied to these particular documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this is a document that would have been received at Kakanj forward command?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's addressed to the command post in Kakanj, and so that's why I put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berbic, I'm going to direct you, again, to a portion of the text that I'd just like you to read out for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, again, on the English, it's the last sentence of the second paragraph under the section entitled "Situation and Activities of 3rd Corps Forces"; and in the B/C/S version, it's the last sentence of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Could you read that sentence out?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. What word does the sentence begin with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The sentence begins with: "The whole numerical strength."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are we? Okay, I see it. Do you see it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, it's the --

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot locate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's the last sentence of the -- do you see the first paragraph on that page, Mr. Berbic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I see here subparagraphs (b), (c), and (d), and there is a paragraph on top without any designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's the top paragraph. I just want to have you to read out the last sentence of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The last sentence is: "Manoeuvring Battalions." I presume that is the sentence. In B/C/S, it begins with: "Manoeuvre Battalions."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The words change in English. That's why the words do not correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you read out that sentence, Mr. Berbic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I can if this is the sentence: "The whole numerical strength of the Manoeuvre Battalions and the El Mujahid Detachment are located in the deployment sectors to conduct reconnaissance and prepare for the forthcoming combat operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02245.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, what is the -- what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: This is a similar document to the previous one. It reads in the title "Daily Regular Combat Report."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what's the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The 16th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And which corps is this documented originating from?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: It says "Command of the 3rd Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And this document is addressed to Kakanj. Now, we've discussed a particular process that would be applied to documents, to daily combat reports arriving in Kakanj. Would that process apply to this document as well?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: The same, yes. Regular daily combat reports are gathered, and then a summary or a joint report is being made. The procedure is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you indicate what role you played in that process?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Given the date of this document, at the time I was still the section desk officer. The person sent to the Operations Centre to work with these reports was usually the head of the security department in Kakanj. If he was unable to go, others would. Therefore, I cannot tell you anything in particular as to what my role was in regard -- as regards this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No, but I'm speaking about in general. In your time in Kakanj, did there come a time when you had a role in terms of daily combat reports?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you indicate what your role was?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: My role was to read the whole report and take note of its contents. And the part referred to as "security situation," I believe it can be found in this report as well. I would extract that portion from all of the reports, and I would have to take out the most important information, put it in summary form; and together with the representatives of other administrations, we were supposed to compile the final report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who was the -- who was the head of the security service in Kakanj at this time, as of the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: He wasn't called "head of the security service." He was called "the head of a part of the security service located at Kakanj." Do you mean that person?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was Mr. Refik Cesko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I would now refer the witness to -- on the English, it's going to be on the top of page 3; and on the B/C/S, it's page 1. It's the last section or the last sentence under the section entitled "The Situation and Activities of the 3rd Corps Forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you see the sentence, Mr. Berbic? It begins: "In the Command of the 35th Division."

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: No. The title reads "The 35th Division" and then follows the text. But I don't see yes see where it says "In the Command of the 35th Division." Now I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's the last sentence. If you could read out the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: "In the Command of the 35th Division, a meeting was held regarding the preparations and carrying out of forthcoming combat activities in which the El Mujahedin Detachment, the 328th Mountain Brigade, and the 329th Mountain Brigade will take part." However, this is not the part of the report that we would usually process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 363.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P03018.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: This document is entitled "Daily Report."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Does it differ from the documents -- is it a different -- does it have a different nature than the documents we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: In form, it is different, and the addressees differ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can we go to page 7 of the B/C/S and page 12 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, do you see -- if you could look at the bottom section of that document, to whom is this document addressed? To whom is it to be delivered?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: It says that it should be delivered to the Security Administration of the Main Staff of the ARBH. Next, I don't know if it says "UB" or "OB," since the acronyms would mean different things then. Perhaps, we can zoom in. "OB KM Kakanj." The third addressee is the 3rd Corps Military Security Service organ, "OAIP." I believe it was the organ that drafted the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you clarify what "OB KM Kakanj" stands for?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: "OB" could mean "Security Organ." "UB" means "Security Administration."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to whom within the Military Security Administration in Kakanj would this document have gone to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was sent to the administration; but to whom exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could go back to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If you'll note, Mr. Berbic, the document is dated the 21st of July, 1995. Do you know, as of that date, does that assist you in answering the question that I just posed to you, in terms of who this document would have gone to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: In the heading, it says "Security Administration, Main Staff of the ARBiH." It is possible that a copy went to Sarajevo and another to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you know -- my question to you was: Do you know whom, within Kakanj, would have received this document? Would it have been treated the same way as the daily combat reports, or would it have been treated in a different way?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I don't know who in Kakanj received this report. If anyone, it must have been someone from the administration in Kakanj. And the procedure with this document would be different, since this document was sent by the security department of the 3rd Corps to the Security Administration. As for the others who compiled daily combat reports and who worked on that, to them this document was not forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, are you familiar with the process that would have been applied to this particular document and which you just referred to in general in your answer?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: This is a document which concerns the Military Security Service. What were the -- what process the document and the information contained in it would undergo from that moment would be indicated by his remark or mark on the document by the head of the administration. That is the procedure that we apply. So there is no team that would be perusing this report; although, a team could be attached for that particular purpose, not perhaps -- not perhaps a complete team, but for the daily report, which is the essential part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that this document be marked for identification. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 364 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, were there instances when you had the responsibility of transmitting information from General Jasarevic to General Delic in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: There were situations where I needed to submit some documents, but in the period from the time when I became -- assumed the post of the head of a part -- of a segment of the Security Administration which was located at the Kakanj command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you indicate when you assumed this post of the head of a part of the segment of the Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was in October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in your -- in a previous answer that you had given, you said: "Where I needed to submit some documents." Can you explain what kinds of documents these were? Can you elaborate on that answer?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: There have been some situations also prior to my assumption of this leading duty at the post, when my superior at the Kakanj command post simply gave me an envelope, and then he would tell me to take it to the DC and that it be handed over there, to the people there. So, at that time, I would just simply take that envelope and take it there, and I did this a couple of times, as did others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who is your superior? Who are you referring to when you say "my superior"?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: My superior during that time period was the head of the section. That was Refik Cesko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And for the purpose of clarification, these documents and envelope -- in the envelope, these would be coming from General Jasarevic in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. The witness said that he would be given a closed -- a sealed envelope, so I don't know how he would be able to tell whether it was from General Jasarevic or from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first question that I posed to the witness was: "Mr. Berbic, were there instances when you had the responsibility of transmitting information from General Jasarevic to General Delic?" And so I just -- the witness had referred to some documents coming in an envelope, and I just wanted to clarify that he understood that my -- that I was still relating to the first question that I had posed to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, can you answer the question that I had posed to you? And the question was whether these documents and envelopes were the ones coming from General Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: So during this period, before I assumed this leading post, I would simply be given sealed envelopes, and I would take them to the DC. I was not privy to what was in it, who was sending what, and to whom. It wasn't important for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was -- okay. Were you given these documents by Mr. Jasarevic or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these documents would be given to me by my immediate superior, Mr. Cesko, to either me, myself, or someone of a similar rank, for us to personally take them so as to avoid the regular channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berbic, can you explain in a little more detail how you would go about transmitting the information to General Delic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was a markedly leading question. He referred to the DC, and he did not refer to General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon. By the way, what did you say the DC is? I know you explained it, but I forgot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, "DC" stands for Distribution Centre." That was the firm previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berbic, just for clarification, who had offices in the DC?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I said, at the beginning, that at the DC were the offices of Commander Delic. He had his office there; the Chief of Staff had, and that was General Hadzihasanovic; as well as some officers of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. I'm going to ask the question I posed to you earlier. I'm going to do it again. How would you go about delivering these documents to the DC and, I suppose, to General Delic's office in the DC?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I took this document with the intention of handing it over -- delivering it to General Delic if he was there, and I didn't know whether he was or not. But in the majority of cases, I would give that document to the Chief of Staff or to one of the Operations Administration officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berbic, once that document was consumed by the -- by whomever you had delivered it to, would you have any further responsibilities in relation to that document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that it wasn't just me that delivered that document or such documents, as actually it was up to the superiors to see to the delivery of documents and the procedure surrounding it. I really am not privy to what happened to the document, at the time, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, I'll ask one more question before we break for the day. We've been referring to these -- we've been referring to them as "documents." Do these documents have a specific name?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC
utterances.text: I had no way of knowing then, when I was given this envelope to take to a specific place, what it was about. I could only assume. What my obligation was, was to directly deliver it, but there was no way of my being able to know what was in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm not speaking of the contents of the document. I'm just speaking about a title that was applied to the document. What was it called, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has repeatedly stated that it was a sealed envelope, so I fail to see how the witness could have seen the title, if I understand the question well, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'll be showing the witness a document which will certainly suggest that he was aware of the title of these documents, and so I wanted to lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, I think you should lay the foundation for that document; and when the witness has seen that document, then you can ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I think you're going in reverse now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. I guess it's past 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is. Okay. Sir, we have come to the end of the day for today. You'll have to come back tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Okay? Court adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24
